verdict.text: Decide on a nowcast, not on the stale snapshot; choose transfers with a rolling scenario LP (falling back to the age-aware rule); and gate every transfer through sender-side quota leases. Across five held-out settings this stack is best or tied-best everywhere, roughly halves cost whenever information is delayed, and makes promising the same unit twice impossible.
verdict.decide_s: Re-solve a 3-day, 16-scenario sample-average LP every day at the hub (about 0.1 s). Field devices run the age-aware rule, which ties the LP when data is fresh.
kpis: cost vs the age-aware rule with a 2-day data delay (0.340 vs 0.652)
units promised twice per year at a 2-day delay, once nowcast and leases are on
cost vs the rule when supply is scarce and lands in one place (1.230 vs 1.635)
best policy's gap to perfect foresight in the default setting (the bound is loose)

findings: Fresh information beats a cleverer optimiser. With a 2- or 4-day delay, deciding on a nowcast roughly halves every policy's cost (age-aware rule: 0.652 → 0.371 at δ = 2, 0.953 → 0.439 at δ = 4).
With fresh data the rule and the LP tie. 0.304 vs 0.299 per unit of demand; paired difference −0.005 ± 0.006, not significant.

Scarcity is where optimisation pays. When supply is 95% of demand and 90% of it lands in one place, the LP is clearly best (1.230 vs 1.635), and the plain age-aware rule is the weakest coordinated policy.
Over-tuning backfires. Constants tuned on six training futures did worse on unseen futures in the default setting (+0.021 ± 0.006). Keep the rule's constants principled.
Leases make conflicts impossible. Tested separately on 20 seeds: conflicts go to exactly zero. Without a nowcast, leases also cut cost 11–23%; with one they are cost-neutral (within ±2%).
Headroom remains. The best policy is 48–73% above the perfect-foresight bound. That bound is loose, so the recoverable gap is smaller; better demand forecasts are the most likely lever.
